column4: The humbled eyes, engulfing humiliation, and recalled call to prostrate while sound make this the section's exact boundary between voluntary worldly bowing and compelled abasement on that Day.
The section explicitly hears prayer inside خَاشِعَةٌ; here the successful believers are خَاشِعُونَ precisely in their prayer, the saving worldly counterpart to the humbled faces of 88:2.
The command فَانصَبْ uses the section's نصب root for rising to strenuous devotion, turning upright weariness into a commanded act rather than the condemned body's exhaustion in 88:3.
يَصْلَى النَّارَ الْكُبْرَى gives the same fire-entering branch heard in 88:4; its proximity to prayer in 87:15 makes the section's two senses audible together.
ذَكَرَ اسْمَ رَبِّهِ فَصَلَّى joins remembrance to the prayer branch of the section's صلى root, opposite the person who يَصْلَى the greater fire in 87:12.
فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّى names failure to affirm and pray at life's closing passage, supplying the refused voluntary prayer behind the later compelled posture.
وَلَكِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى makes denial and turning away the sequel to not praying in 75:31, directly clarifying the turner-away of 88:23.
The summons to prostrate when they can no longer do so supplies the immediate Last-Day action completed by the humbled eyes and remembered earlier summons in 68:43.
خَاشِعَةً أَبْصَارُهُمْ and humiliation covering them on the promised Day closely restage the section's humbled faces as involuntary exposure.
خُشَّعًا أَبْصَارُهُمْ places humbled eyes on people emerging from the graves, fixing the section's bodily inclination within resurrection rather than voluntary worship.
The condemned are shown to the Fire خَاشِعِينَ مِنَ الذُّلِّ and looking furtively; humiliation, lowered sight, and exposure to fire converge as they do across 88:2-4.
أَبْصَارُهَا خَاشِعَةٌ gives the same humbled gaze amid the resurrection shock, another direct staging of the section's compulsory bodily humility.
On that Day even voices خَشَعَتْ before the Merciful until only a whisper is heard, extending the section's forced visible humility from faces to speech.
Faces are turned about in the Fire while their owners wish they had obeyed Allah and the Messenger, joining the punished face to regret over refused obedience.
Being dragged on their faces into the Fire literalizes the section's bond between an abased body and burning.
Faces are cast down into the Fire and the sufferers are told they receive what they did, making bodily inversion the disclosed outcome of action.
Gathering people on their faces toward Hell makes the face's downward posture part of their compulsory journey to fire.
The Last-Day gathering on faces, followed in the same ayah by Hell as abode, directly combines bodily abasement and fire.
The Fire scorches their faces and leaves them grimacing, presenting the face itself as the site where burning becomes visible.
The disbelievers cannot keep the Fire from their faces or backs, showing the total bodily helplessness implicit in the section's compelled posture.
Fire covering their faces supplies a compact parallel to the sequence from faces in 88:2 to burning in 88:4.
The person forced to shield the evil punishment with his face embodies the loss of bodily freedom that distinguishes Last-Day abasement from chosen prostration.
At death the angels strike the disbelievers' faces and backs and make them taste burning punishment, linking the death-setting around 75:31-32 to the section's face-and-fire scene.
On the Day when faces darken, those faces are addressed for disbelief and told to taste punishment; the face reveals the inward refusal before punishment follows.
Their answer, that they were not among those who prayed, places omitted صلاة as the first stated reason for reaching Saqar in 74:42.
The question مَا سَلَكَكُمْ فِي سَقَرَ names the fire whose first answer is failure to pray in 74:43, recreating the section's prayer/fire junction across adjacent ayat.

Their so-called prayer at the House is only whistling and clapping, and the ayah immediately orders them to taste punishment; it marks the boundary between the posture or label of صلاة and true worship.
The Prophet is told he is not a compeller over them and must remind by the Quran whoever fears the warning, an especially close parallel to the reminder-without-control stance of 88:21-22.
لَا يَصْلَاهَا إِلَّا الْأَشْقَى uses the fire-entering sense of صلى and is immediately defined by denial and turning away in 92:16.
الَّذِي كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّى identifies the one who burns as the one who denied and turned away, almost exactly unpacking the movement from 88:23 to punishment.
These people let no trade distract them from remembrance and prayer because they fear a Day when hearts and eyes overturn; chosen remembrance and صلاة answer the future upheaval of the face.
رُكَّعًا سُجَّدًا and the mark of prostration on their faces unite voluntary bowing, prostration, and the face, reversing the section's compelled mark of humiliation.
Creation prostrates to Allah, while the same ayah distinguishes many people for whom punishment is due; it puts submission and punishment on the exact boundary the section explores.
Prayer is described as heavy except for الْخَاشِعِينَ, explicitly joining صلاة to the section's خشع root and showing inward humility making the bodily act possible.
The command to establish prayer and bow with those who bow gives the Quranic act behind the section's dictionary statement that the humble one is also the one in rukūʿ.
Mary is commanded to be devout, prostrate, and bow with those who bow, gathering the voluntary worship postures sounded by the section.
Those who establish prayer are described while bowing, making the prayer-rukūʿ relation explicit in a single ayah.
The command to bow, prostrate, and worship the Lord lays out the voluntary bodily sequence that the section hears beside bending and burning.
When they are told ارْكَعُوا they do not bow; this refused worldly rukūʿ is the sharp reversal behind the inevitable lowered posture on the Last Day.
All in the heavens and earth prostrate willingly or unwillingly, expressly stating the voluntary/compelled boundary that the section finds between worship now and abasement then.
The night worshipper alternates prostration and standing while fearing the Hereafter and hoping for mercy; purposeful qiyām and sujūd oppose the exhausted body carried unknowingly into fire.
The servants of the Merciful spend the night prostrating and standing before their Lord, combining the two voluntary postures whose sounds the section detects.
Immediately after their prostration and standing, they ask that Hell's punishment be turned away, explicitly placing worship posture against burning punishment.
The call for believers' hearts to تَخْشَعَ at Allah's remembrance makes humility a voluntary present response to reminder, before it becomes an imposed outward condition.
Those who truly believe respond to being reminded of the signs by falling in prostration without arrogance, the voluntary response sought by the reminder in 88:21.
أَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ لِذِكْرِي directly joins prayer to remembrance, supporting the section's dictionary sense of ذكر as prayer while preserving both ideas.
Prayer restrains indecency and Allah's remembrance is greater, another explicit meeting of صلاة and ذكر that explains why the section can hear remembrance within prayer.
When the call to Friday prayer is made, believers are commanded to hasten to ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ, a Quranic setting in which remembrance names the act of communal prayer.
After prayer, Allah is to be remembered standing, sitting, and lying, then prayer re-established; remembrance and bodily positions are held together rather than reduced to posture.
Guarding the prayers is paired with standing devoutly before Allah, giving the voluntary upright worship that the section hears inside نَاصِبَةٌ.
The humble men and women and those who remember Allah much share one promise of forgiveness and reward, joining the section's خشع and ذكر motifs on the saving side.
They fall on their faces weeping and the revelation increases their خُشُوعًا, showing a face lowered voluntarily through receptive remembrance rather than humiliation.
فَذَكِّرْ إِنْ نَفَعَتِ الذِّكْرَى gives the parallel command to remind that opens the same nearby sequence ending in fire or prayer.
The one who fears will remember, supplying the receptive hearer of the reminder before 87:15 joins remembering the Lord's name to prayer.
The most wretched avoids the reminder and then enters the greater Fire, tracing the refusal that lies between reminder and burning.
Success belongs to the one who purifies himself, introducing the person who remembers and prays in 87:15 as the saving counterpart to the burner in 87:12.
The wrongdoer is reminded of his Lord's signs and then turns away from them; this condenses the movement from the command to remind in 88:21 to turning away in 88:23.
Whoever turns away from Allah's remembrance receives a constricted life and is raised blind, making refusal of ذكر become compelled deprivation at resurrection.
The command to remind because reminder benefits believers identifies the receptive audience for the same prophetic act commanded in 88:21.
The question asks why they turn away from التَّذْكِرَةِ, directly coupling reminder with the very motion of refusal developed beside 88:21-23.
No thirst, fatigue نَصَبٌ, or hunger borne in Allah's path goes unwritten as a righteous deed; this is purposeful, credited weariness against the exhausted body ending in fire.
Paradise is a place where no نَصَبٌ touches its people, the direct reversal of the weary condition named by نَاصِبَةٌ in 88:3.
The inhabitants of the lasting home praise Allah because neither نَصَبٌ nor weariness touches them, setting enduring relief against the section's exhausted condemned body.
Hypocrites stand for prayer lazily, showing off, and remember Allah only a little; the ayah exposes how an upright prayer posture can remain spiritually empty.
Their offerings are rejected because they come to prayer only lazily and spend unwillingly, another boundary between performing صلاة bodily and submitting willingly.
Woe is pronounced over people still called الْمُصَلِّينَ, warning that the prayer-name and posture alone do not prevent the condemned outcome.
Those worshippers are heedless of their own prayer, specifying the inward failure that lets prayer-shaped action remain empty.
Their display for other people completes the boundary: visible worship posture can be directed toward an audience rather than toward God.
Successors who neglected prayer and followed desires will meet ruin, directly connecting abandoned صلاة with a punitive end.
The command قُمِ اللَّيْلَ makes prolonged standing a chosen night devotion, the Quranic qiyām heard alongside the section's definition of upright exertion.
Remembering the Lord's name and devoting oneself wholly follows the night-standing command, paralleling the remembrance-and-prayer sequence in 87:15.
Allah acknowledges the Prophet and a group standing through large portions of the night and then grants a practicable measure, distinguishing measured devotion from endless exhaustion.
The command to remember the Lord's name morning and evening begins a compact sequence in which remembrance leads into nighttime prostration.
Prostration during the night and long glorification give the bodily worship that completes the remembrance command of 76:25.
The خَاشِعِينَ of 2:45 are those who expect to meet their Lord and return to Him, grounding voluntary humility in awareness of the very encounter where false refusal ends.
Allah could send a sign that would leave their necks permanently bowed to it; this hypothetical forced submission clarifies why the prophetic reminder leaves room for a voluntary response.
The Prophet is asked whether he would compel people to believe when Allah could have made all believe, defining the no-compulsion side of the section's reminder and later forced abasement.
Everything in the heavens and earth submits to Allah willingly or unwillingly and returns to Him, expressing both the choice now and the unavoidable return behind the section's two kinds of bending.
Created things cast inclining shadows that prostrate to Allah while abased, turning visible downward inclination into a sign of universal submission.
When the Quran is recited to them they do not prostrate, another direct refusal of voluntary sujūd before the Day when bodily abasement cannot be refused.
The passage singles out one who forbids, setting human resistance against the servant's prayer in 96:10 and the final command to prostrate.
عَبْدًا إِذَا صَلَّى identifies the forbidden act as a servant's prayer, placing chosen صلاة under opposition rather than abandonment.
The servant is told not to obey the opponent but to prostrate and draw near, making voluntary downward movement the route to nearness.
The direct command to prostrate to Allah and worship states the willing bodily response whose refusal later becomes compulsory abasement.
Zechariah's household call on Allah in hope and fear and are خَاشِعِينَ toward Him, a devotional use of the section's root outside formal prayer posture.
They rush from the graves as if toward a نُصُب; this different noun of the section's نصب root stands immediately before their humbled eyes in 70:44, placing an erected goal beside lowered bodies.
A mountain would be seen خَاشِعًا and split from fear if the Quran descended upon it; the imagined humbled object exposes the hardness of a hearer who resists reminder.
Humanity will stand before the Lord of the worlds on the Day of resurrection, making standing then an imposed summons rather than chosen qiyām in worship.
The drive that day is to the Lord, so the subsequent denial, turning away, and failure to pray are framed by a return the denier cannot resist.
The soul reaching the collarbones locates the later statement that he neither affirmed nor prayed at the closing threshold when voluntary action is ending.
The travellers say that their journey has brought them نَصَبًا, giving the ordinary bodily fatigue from which the section's description of نَاصِبَةٌ draws.
Job names نُصْبٍ and torment as an affliction that has touched him, showing exhausted suffering in worldly trial rather than as the fixed Last-Day condition.
Every human is laboring strenuously toward the Lord and will meet Him; this gives the unavoidable destination of work and weariness without assuming that every exertion is worship.
Their striving is lost in worldly life while they think they are doing well, a concrete parallel for exertion whose outward labor does not yield salvation.
Their deeds come to nothing because they denied the signs and the meeting with their Lord, explaining the failed destination of the lost striving in 18:104.
The question about the greatest losers in deeds plausibly opens a reading of 88:3 as futile exertion, though the section itself develops bodily weariness more explicitly than lost works.
Those too proud for Allah's worship will enter Hell abased, directly turning refused voluntary worship into compulsory humiliation and fire.
The revealed rule that punishment falls on whoever denies and turns away closely restates the movement from 88:23 to 88:24.
This ayah identifies the threatened destination as a blazing Fire, beginning a passage that names turning away and then exempts those devoted to prayer.
The blaze calls the person who turned his back and turned away, supplying the refusal that connects its fire in 70:15 with the prayerful exception in 70:22.
The worshippers are expressly excepted from the preceding fiery outcome, another direct Quranic junction between صلاة and burning.
Constancy in prayer defines the worshippers excepted from the blaze, showing sustained willing devotion rather than a momentary bodily pose.
Guarding their prayer repeats the passage's decisive attribute before their honored destination is named, making care for صلاة the counterpart to turning away.
Those who guard prayer are honored in gardens, completing the outcome opposite both the blaze earlier in the passage and the humbled eyes in 70:44.
When commanded to prostrate to the Merciful, they question the command and recoil; their refusal sharply contrasts with the willing nighttime prostration in 25:64.
When the Merciful's signs are recited, the prophets fall prostrate and weep; this receptive posture is the immediate opposite of the successors who neglect prayer in 19:59.
The earth is seen خَاشِعَةً and then stirred to life by water, a secondary use in which low stillness is receptive and revivable rather than punitive humiliation.
The command to enjoin prayer on one's family and persevere in it presents صلاة as sustained exertion whose provision and outcome remain with Allah.
The command to establish prayer is followed by the assurance that good deeds remove evils and that this is a reminder for those who remember, joining صلاة and ذكر with an effective moral result.
Allah sees the Prophet when he rises or stands; the following movement among those prostrating makes worshipful standing a likely, though context-dependent, contribution here.
The Prophet's movement among those prostrating places his bodily action within a worshipping community, completing the standing scene of 26:218.
Angels call Zechariah while he stands praying in the sanctuary, explicitly uniting upright posture with صلاة.
Bowing and prostrating appear among the defining qualities of faithful worshippers, making those postures signs of a whole obedient life.
The command to remember the Lord inwardly with humility and fear makes ذكر a quiet voluntary lowering of the self before the prostration of 7:206.
Those near the Lord are not arrogant about worshipping Him; they glorify Him and prostrate, opposing pride with willing bodily submission.
After the prayer ends, believers disperse and continue remembering Allah much, showing both the prayer sense of ذكر in 62:9 and remembrance extending beyond the rite.
Woe belongs to hearts hardened against Allah's remembrance, the exact inward reversal of a heart humbling voluntarily to reminder.
Revelation makes skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften toward Allah's remembrance, a specific bodily response to ذكر that stops short of forced abasement.
The Prophet is told to turn from whoever turns from Allah's remembrance and wants only worldly life, identifying the present refusal behind later humiliation.
If they turn away, the Prophet is told he was not sent as their guardian and owes only conveyance, closely matching reminder without control in 88:21-23.
If they turn away, the Messenger's duty is only clear conveyance, another precise limit on the reminder's authority before judgment.
On the Day of resurrection liars against Allah have blackened faces, and the ayah locates the arrogant in Hell; face, pride, and punishment converge.
When the promised event draws near, the disbelievers' faces become distressed and they are told this is what they demanded, making the face disclose belated recognition.
Faces on that Day have dust upon them, beginning another judgment portrait in which the condemned condition is visibly borne by the face.
Darkness covers those dusty faces, adding an engulfing visible abasement before their owners are identified in 80:42.
The dusty, darkened faces belong to disbelieving transgressors, tying the Last-Day facial state to their prior refusal.
Radiant faces on that Day provide a direct reversal of the humbled condemned faces in the section.
Those radiant faces look toward their Lord, showing chosen faith culminating in an uplifted gaze rather than the lowered gaze of humiliation.
Other faces on that Day are gloomy, a close facial counterpart to the section's humbled faces within the same surah that names failure to pray.
Those gloomy faces expect a crushing calamity, making their posture and expression the bodily anticipation of punishment.
Shackles around necks and chains by which people are dragged portray the condemned body placed under compulsory restraint before the burning in 40:72.
They are dragged into boiling water and then burned in the Fire, completing the forced bodily movement begun in 40:71.
The deviators are toppled headlong into Hell, another concrete loss of bodily control at entry into punishment.
Walking fallen on one's face is contrasted with walking upright on a straight path, making downward and upright posture disclose two contrary orientations before their final outcomes.
Iblis refuses the command to prostrate and grounds the refusal in superiority, making pride the motive for rejecting voluntary lowering.
After refusing prostration, Iblis is ordered down because arrogance is forbidden there and is cast among the debased, turning self-exaltation into compulsory lowliness.
The same refusal passage ends with Hell being filled by Iblis and his followers, supplying the fiery outcome beyond the forced descent in 7:13.
The resistant hearer turns his back and grows arrogant, a bodily and inward refusal that leads directly toward Saqar in 74:26.
The threat to burn him in Saqar uses the section's fire-entering branch of صلى and supplies the outcome of the arrogance and turning in 74:23.
Luqman commands his son to establish prayer and patiently bear what befalls him, joining صلاة to purposeful endurance rather than futile exhaustion.
During the danger prayer, one group's completed prostration marks its turn in the صلاة, a Quranic instance of prayer concretely constituted by bodily sujūd.
A human being has only what he strives for, setting accountable, owned effort against an image of exhausted labor whose value is in question.
Each person's striving will be seen, so bodily exertion cannot conceal its direction or purpose at judgment.
Striving will then be fully repaid, completing the reversal in which meaningful effort receives its exact outcome rather than merely ending in fatigue.
Every creature and the angels prostrate to Allah without arrogance, extending the inclining shadows of 16:48 into conscious willing submission.
They fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded, supplying the obedient inward stance behind the prostration of 16:49.
The command forbids prostration to sun or moon and directs it to their Creator, marking correct worship by both bodily act and rightful object.
The Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord's praise and be among those who prostrate, coupling spoken praise with voluntary bodily lowering.
The command to worship until certainty arrives makes the prostration of 15:98 a lifelong stance maintained up to death.
The sanctuary is purified for those circling, standing, bowing, and prostrating, gathering all the worship postures sounded by the section into one sacred scene.
Believers remember Allah while standing, sitting, and lying down, showing ذكر inhabiting every bodily orientation rather than depending on one posture.
Allah's servant stands calling upon Him while a crowd presses around; this may preserve worshipful qiyām, though the ayah itself says invocation rather than explicitly naming formal prayer.
